title: Models and the Particle Model of Matter
competency: Explain the properties of solids, liquids, and gases and the processes involved in changes of state using the particle model of matter.
objectives: Recognize that scientists use models to explain phenomena that cannot be easily seen.
Describe the Particle Model of Matter.
Explain how particles behave in the three states of matter.
Illustrate the changes of state in terms of particle arrangement and energy.
introduction: In Science, we often deal with things that are too small to be seen by the naked eye, like atoms and molecules. To understand these, scientists create 'Models.' One of the most important models in Chemistry is the Particle Model of Matter, which helps us explain why water can be a solid (ice), a liquid, or a gas (steam).
content:
1. Why use Scientific Models?

Models are representations of objects or systems. Scientists use them to visualize, explain, and predict phenomena. For example, a globe is a model of the Earth, and a diagram of an atom is a model of subatomic particles.

2. The Particle Model of Matter

This model is based on four key principles:

  • All matter is made up of tiny particles.
  • Particles are constantly in motion.
  • There are spaces between particles.
  • Particles attract each other.

3. States of Matter

  • Solids: Particles are closely packed in a fixed arrangement. They vibrate but do not move out of place. This gives solids a definite shape and volume.
  • Liquids: Particles are close together but can slide past one another. They have a definite volume but take the shape of their container.
  • Gases: Particles are far apart and move rapidly in all directions. They have no definite shape or volume.

4. Changes of State

When heat is added or removed, the energy of the particles changes, leading to a change of state:

  • Melting (Solid to Liquid): Particles gain energy and break free from fixed positions.
  • Evaporation (Liquid to Gas): Particles gain enough energy to fly apart.
  • Condensation (Gas to Liquid): Particles lose energy and cluster together.
  • Freezing (Liquid to Solid): Particles lose energy and lock into fixed positions.

examples.title: Diffusion
examples.description: When you spray perfume in one corner of a room, the scent eventually reaches the other side. This is because gas particles move randomly and spread out.

examples.title: Expansion of Bridges
examples.description: Bridges are built with 'expansion joints' (gaps) because in hot weather, the particles in the metal move faster and push further apart, causing the bridge to expand.

keyTerms.definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
The energy of motion; higher temperature means higher kinetic energy.
A physical change from one state of matter to another.

keyConcepts: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles.
The arrangement of particles determines the physical properties of a substance.
Changes of state involve a change in energy, not a change in the type of particles.
summary: The Particle Model of Matter explains that everything is made of moving particles. By understanding how these particles attract each other and move with heat, we can explain the properties of solids, liquids, and gases, as well as how they change from one form to another.

selfCheck.q: What happens to the motion of particles when the temperature increases?
selfCheck.a: The particles move faster (gain kinetic energy).

selfCheck.q: Which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape?
True or False: In a solid, particles are completely still.
selfCheck.a: False. They vibrate in fixed positions.
